author: reek
body: An AUTHENTICATED TLS 1.3 handshake over a reliable stream, end to end, with no network -- and then application data carried both ways under the application traffic keys. This is what an https fetch needs: a client that speaks real TLS to a server it can authenticate, so an https fetch is no longer a refusal.

author: reek
body: The server presents the same real Ed25519 leaf certificate the DTLS loopback uses (minted outside Codex; signatures by our RFC-8032-gated Ed25519). The client carries the CA as its trust anchor and REQUIRES authentication. The negative at the end proves it: a man in the middle who substitutes the ServerHello key share makes the client derive different handshake keys, so it cannot even decrypt the server's encrypted flight, and it never completes.

author: reek
body: Flight 1: the client's ClientHello, in the clear.

author: reek
body: The server answers with ServerHello in the clear and then EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished, each encrypted under the server handshake key.

author: reek
body: The client consumes the flight in order: ServerHello (key agreement), then the encrypted EncryptedExtensions, Certificate (chain walk to the anchor), CertificateVerify (signature over its own transcript), and the server Finished, at which point it emits its own encrypted Finished.

author: reek
body: GET goes up under the client application key; the server decrypts it. A reply goes back down under the server application key; the client decrypts that. This is the byte an https fetch would carry, and until this point in the tree no connection could carry it.

author: reek
body: Flip a byte inside the ServerHello key share. The client derives a different shared secret, so its handshake keys do not match the server's, the encrypted flight will not decrypt, and it never completes.

target: section:The Right Certificate, The Wrong Host
author: reek
body: The negative that makes the positive mean something. This is the SAME server, the SAME genuine certificate and the SAME trust anchor -- the only thing that changes is who the client says it dialled. A client that expected `evil.codex.test` is handed a valid, unexpired, correctly signed certificate for `device.codex.test`, and it must NOT authenticate.

author: reek
body: Before 2026-07-26 it did. The chain walked to the anchor, nothing compared the leaf against the name, and `authenticated` came back True for a certificate belonging to somebody else. Every loopback in the tree passed throughout, because they all agree on a name none of them checked.
